exercises.title: Data Catalog Navigation Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for navigating data catalogs: finding datasets, reading catalog entries, understanding data ownership, quality scores, and freshness metadata.

questions.q: In a data catalog, "the data owner is" refers to:
options: The cloud provider that physically stores the dataset on its infrastructure.
The person or team accountable for the accuracy, quality, and appropriate use of a dataset - they are the primary contact for questions, access requests, and governance decisions.
The data engineer who originally wrote the pipeline that created the dataset.
The executive sponsor who approved the budget for the data platform.
questions.explanation: "Data owner" is a formal governance role. In a catalog entry (DataHub, Atlan, OpenMetadata), the owner field identifies who is accountable - often a domain team lead or product manager, not the engineer who built the pipeline. When you need to request access or understand business context, the data owner is your first point of contact. Distinct from "data steward" (who manages day-to-day quality) and "data custodian" (who manages technical storage).

questions.q: When a catalog entry shows "last updated: 3 days ago", this metadata indicates:
options: The documentation for the dataset was edited 3 days ago by a catalog administrator.
The dataset's data was last refreshed or written to 3 days ago - helping consumers assess freshness and decide whether the data is current enough for their use case.
The schema of the dataset was last modified 3 days ago with a column addition.
The dataset's access control list was reviewed and approved 3 days ago.
questions.explanation: "Last updated" (or "last ingested", "last refreshed") is an operational metadata field that tracks data freshness. If you need daily data and the catalog shows "last updated: 3 days ago", you know there is a potential freshness issue before even querying the table. Data observability tools (Monte Carlo, Soda) monitor this and alert when freshness SLAs are breached. This metadata is distinct from schema change history.

questions.q: A "quality score" in a data catalog entry typically represents:
options: A subjective rating given by users who have queried the dataset recently.
A computed metric - often combining completeness, freshness, validity, and consistency checks - that gives consumers a quick indication of how reliable the dataset is for production use.
The number of times a dataset has passed a manual data audit review.
A compliance score indicating how well the dataset meets GDPR requirements.
questions.explanation: Quality scores in catalogs (e.g., Atlan's "trust score", DataHub's assertions, Great Expectations integrations) aggregate automated data quality checks into a single indicator. A high score means recent checks for null rates, referential integrity, value distribution, and freshness all passed. Consumers can filter catalog search results by quality score to find datasets that are safe to rely on - avoiding the common pitfall of building on poorly-understood data.

questions.q: When searching a data catalog, which action best describes "finding a dataset"?
options: Running a SQL query against the data warehouse to discover tables matching a naming pattern.

Using the catalog's search interface to query by business term, tag, domain, or column name - then reading the catalog entry to understand context, ownership, quality, and lineage before deciding to use it.
Asking a colleague which table to query for a given business question.
Browsing the database schema browser in your SQL client to explore available tables.
questions.explanation: The key differentiator of a data catalog over a raw schema browser is business context. You can search for "customer revenue" and find the dataset because it has been tagged with a business glossary term - even if the underlying table is named "fct_rev_by_cust_mthly". The catalog entry then tells you: owner, quality score, freshness, upstream lineage, certified status, and usage popularity. This is "data discovery" in the governance sense.

questions.q: A "certified" dataset badge in a data catalog communicates:
options: The dataset has been encrypted and meets security certification standards.

The dataset has passed a formal review process - typically including documentation completeness, data quality checks, and owner sign-off - and is endorsed as the authoritative, production-ready source for a given business concept.
The dataset is certified to contain personally identifiable information and must be handled with care.
The dataset's pipeline has been certified by the cloud provider for enterprise SLA guarantees.
questions.explanation: "Certified" (or "verified", "endorsed") status in a catalog (DataHub, Atlan, Alation) means the dataset is the single source of truth for a concept. It has been reviewed by the data owner, documented, and quality-tested. Teams building dashboards or ML models should prefer certified datasets. The inverse - "deprecated" - signals teams to migrate away. This certification lifecycle is central to data governance programs.

exercises.title: Data Catalog Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for data catalogs (DataHub, Atlan, OpenMetadata, Alation), business glossary, data domains, data stewards, dataset certification, and data product concepts.

questions.q: A data catalog is most accurately described as:
options: A database storing only the schemas and table definitions from a data warehouse.

A centralised inventory of all data assets in an organisation - including metadata, lineage, quality signals, ownership, and business context - enabling data discovery, trust, and governance at scale.
A tool for scheduling and orchestrating data pipeline runs across an organisation.
A data quality monitoring platform that tracks anomalies in production datasets.
questions.explanation: Modern data catalogs (DataHub, Atlan, OpenMetadata, Alation) are "the Google for your data": they make datasets discoverable, contextualised, and trustworthy. Without a catalog, engineers spend hours asking "does a table for this exist?" and analysts build shadow spreadsheets instead of using official data.

questions.q: A business glossary in a data catalog maps:
options: Technical column names in the database to their human-readable display names.

Business concepts ("Active User", "Revenue", "Churn") to precise technical definitions and the specific tables/columns that implement them - bridging the gap between business language and data engineering reality.
Internal company jargon to standard industry terminology used in external communications.
Data catalog search queries to the most commonly accessed datasets in the organisation.
questions.explanation: Business glossary example: "Active User = a user who logged in at least once in the last 30 days AND completed at least one core action, as defined in fact_user_activity.is_active." Without this, finance calculates revenue one way, sales another - the glossary enforces a single definition across teams.

questions.q: A data steward's primary responsibility is:
options: Maintaining the physical infrastructure on which data is stored and processed.
Owning the quality, definition, and usage policies for specific data assets - ensuring they are accurate, well-documented, and governed - typically a business domain expert, not an engineer.
Writing and maintaining the data pipelines that load data into the warehouse.
Managing user access permissions for datasets and enforcing data security policies.
questions.explanation: Data stewards bridge business and engineering: they answer "What does this field mean?", "Is this data reliable?", "When should it be deleted?", "Who can access it?". The steward is accountable when data quality issues occur - not the engineer who built the pipeline.

questions.q: A "certified dataset" in a data catalog means:
options: A dataset that has been encrypted and secured to meet compliance certification requirements.

A dataset that has been reviewed and formally approved by a data owner or governance team as reliable, well-documented, and recommended for use - distinguishing it from unverified or experimental datasets.
A dataset stored in a certified cloud region that meets data residency regulations.
A dataset that has passed automated schema validation checks in the data pipeline.
questions.explanation: Certification signals trust: "This dataset is production-quality, owned, documented, and tested." Uncertified datasets may be experiments, work-in-progress, or deprecated assets. Catalogs display certification badges and can filter to certified-only datasets, guiding analysts toward trusted data.

questions.q: The "data product" concept in a data catalog context refers to:
options: A commercial product built on top of company data that is sold to external customers.
A curated, owned, documented, and SLA-backed data asset treated with the same discipline as a software product - with a named owner, quality guarantees, versioning, and a defined consumer interface.
A data dashboard or report delivered to business stakeholders as a product deliverable.
A marketplace listing where datasets can be purchased from third-party data providers.
questions.explanation: Data products (core to data mesh) apply product thinking to data: a team owns "the orders data product", guarantees freshness SLAs, publishes a stable schema interface, handles versioning, and is accountable to consumers. This contrasts with the traditional model where data was a by-product of operational systems.

exercises.title: Data Lineage Basics Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for data lineage definition, upstream vs. downstream datasets, lineage graphs, column-level lineage, and impact analysis.

questions.q: Data lineage is best described as:
options: The history of who has owned and administered a database over time.
The complete record of where data originates and every transformation it undergoes as it flows through systems - enabling teams to trace any output back to its source.
The network topology of database servers and their replication relationships.
The version history of a data schema as it evolves across releases.
questions.explanation: Data lineage answers "Where did this number come from?" and "How was it transformed?" It is foundational to debugging data quality issues, understanding impact of changes, and meeting regulatory audit requirements (BCBS 239, GDPR). Tools: OpenLineage, Marquez, Atlas, modern data catalogs.

questions.q: In a data pipeline, an "upstream" dataset is:
options: A dataset stored in a higher-cost, premium storage tier.
A source dataset that feeds data into the current table - changing an upstream dataset can affect all tables that depend on it.
A dataset that has been promoted to a certified, production-ready state.
A dataset that is physically located closer to the data source in network terms.
questions.explanation: Upstream = earlier in the data flow (closer to the source). Downstream = later (closer to the consumer). If the orders table is upstream of the monthly_revenue model, any schema change to orders can break monthly_revenue. Lineage graphs visualise these dependency chains.

questions.q: Column-level lineage tracks:
options: The access permissions granted to individual columns in a data warehouse.
Not just which tables a dataset depends on, but specifically which source columns were used to compute each output column - enabling precise impact analysis.
The data types and constraints applied to each column in a table schema.
The business owner responsible for each column in a certified dataset.
questions.explanation: Column-level lineage is far more precise than table-level lineage. Example: "revenue_usd in the weekly_summary table is derived from amount_cents in raw.orders divided by 100, filtered where status = 'completed'". This enables targeted impact analysis - if amount_cents changes, you know exactly which output columns are affected.

questions.q: Impact analysis in the context of data lineage means:
options: Assessing the business impact of a data outage on revenue and operations.
Using the lineage graph to answer "if I change or deprecate this table/column, which downstream reports, dashboards, and models will be affected?" - before making the change.
Analysing the performance impact of a data pipeline on database query latency.
Measuring the impact of data quality issues on the accuracy of business metrics.
questions.explanation: "Which reports are affected if I change this table?" is the classic impact analysis question. Without lineage, engineers must grep code repositories and ask colleagues. With lineage: navigate the graph, see all downstream consumers, notify owners proactively. This prevents silent data breakages.

questions.q: The OpenLineage specification is:
options: An open-source data catalog for discovering and documenting datasets.
A vendor-neutral open standard for capturing and emitting data lineage events from pipelines, enabling lineage data to be collected by any compatible backend regardless of the tool that produced it.
An open-source alternative to commercial data warehouse solutions like Snowflake.
A specification for defining data quality rules in a portable, tool-agnostic format.
questions.explanation: OpenLineage (openlineage.io) standardises lineage event emission: Spark jobs, Airflow DAGs, dbt runs all emit lineage in the same format. Marquez is the reference backend. This solves the fragmentation problem where each tool had its own lineage format, making cross-tool lineage impossible.

exercises.title: Data Observability Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for data observability (Monte Carlo, Acceldata), data downtime, freshness, volume, distribution, schema change detection, data incidents, and data health dashboards.

questions.q: Data observability is best described as:
options: The ability to observe how analysts are using data assets across an organisation.

The ability to understand the health and reliability of data across the data stack - detecting, resolving, and preventing data quality issues by monitoring freshness, volume, distribution, schema, and lineage continuously.
A compliance practice that makes data processing activities observable and auditable by regulators.
The capability to observe query performance metrics in a data warehouse or data lake.
questions.explanation: Data observability (coined by Barr Moses, Monte Carlo) is the data equivalent of software observability. Just as engineers use logs, metrics, and traces to understand system health, data teams use observability to understand data health. The five pillars: freshness, volume, distribution, schema, lineage.

questions.q: "Data downtime" in observability terminology means:
options: Scheduled maintenance windows when data warehouse is unavailable for queries.
Periods when data is missing, inaccurate, or otherwise unreliable - analogous to service downtime in software reliability: the time during which data consumers cannot trust the data they are seeing.
The time it takes for data to be processed from ingestion to availability in the warehouse.
Network downtime affecting data transfer between source systems and the data platform.
questions.explanation: Monte Carlo popularised "data downtime" as a metric: how many hours per month is data in a bad state? Like measuring system availability as 99.9% uptime, teams can track data reliability. High data downtime = analysts are frequently querying data they cannot trust, making decisions on bad information.

questions.q: Schema change detection in data observability monitors:
options: Changes to user access permissions and role assignments in the data warehouse.
Automatic detection of unexpected changes to table structures - added, removed, or renamed columns, changed data types - that can silently break downstream pipelines and dashboards.
Detecting when a data schema fails to comply with the organisation's naming standards.
Monitoring schema version migrations to ensure they are applied in the correct order.
questions.explanation: Schema changes are a leading cause of data incidents: a source team renames a column from "user_id" to "account_id" without warning; downstream joins silently return nulls; reports show $0 revenue for a week before anyone notices. Observability platforms detect schema diffs and alert immediately, before downstream breakage.

questions.q: In data observability, "distribution monitoring" tracks:
options: How data is distributed across cloud regions and availability zones for resilience.

The statistical distribution of values in key columns - detecting when a column's value range, null rate, or frequency distribution changes significantly from its historical baseline, indicating possible data quality issues.
How query load is distributed across compute nodes in a distributed data warehouse.
The distribution of data ownership responsibilities across teams and data stewards.
questions.explanation: Distribution monitoring example: "the revenue column historically has values between $10 and $50,000; today 2% of values are above $1,000,000." This could indicate a currency unit error (cents vs dollars), a fraud pattern, or a pipeline bug. Static rules cannot catch this - ML-based distribution monitoring learns expected ranges.

questions.q: A "data incident" in a data observability context is:
options: A security breach where unauthorised users access confidential data assets.

A detected data quality failure affecting data consumers - wrong values, missing data, stale data, or broken pipelines - managed with an incident response process similar to software production incidents.
An accidental deletion of production data requiring restoration from backup.
A governance violation where data was used outside of its approved policy scope.
questions.explanation: Data incidents follow the same lifecycle as production incidents: detection → triage → root cause analysis → resolution → post-mortem. "The orders table had null revenue for 4 hours due to a CDC connector restart - impact: 3 dashboards showed incorrect data, 1 automated alert fired incorrectly." Teams track MTTR (Mean Time To Resolution) for data incidents.

exercises.title: Data Provenance Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practice data provenance vocabulary: provenance chain, external vendor data, immutable audit logs, proving data origin for regulatory purposes, and chain of custody language.

questions.q: What does 'data provenance' mean?
options: The speed at which data is processed
The complete record of where data came from and how it was transformed
The format in which data is stored
The frequency of data pipeline runs
questions.explanation: Data provenance is the documented history of data's origin, movement, and transformations. It answers: where did this data come from, who touched it, and how was it changed?

questions.q: An auditor asks you to prove that sales data 'came from external vendor X on date Y.' What record type supports this?
options: A query execution plan
An immutable audit log with timestamped data ingestion records
A data dictionary entry
A pipeline performance dashboard
questions.explanation: An immutable audit log records exactly when data was received, from which source, and by whom - providing the evidence needed for regulatory or legal proof of data origin.

questions.q: What is a 'provenance chain'?
options: A blockchain used to store all company data
The unbroken sequence of documented steps showing data's journey from origin to current state
A chain of approvals needed to access a dataset
A list of data owners in a department
questions.explanation: A provenance chain is the complete, unbroken sequence of records showing every step data has taken - from original source through all transformations - providing full traceability.

questions.q: The phrase 'chain of custody' in a data context means:
options: The network of data centers holding replicas
The documented sequence of who had control over data at each point in its lifecycle
The order of SQL joins in a query
The hierarchy of database permissions
questions.explanation: Chain of custody (borrowed from legal/forensic contexts) means a documented, verifiable record of every person or system that had possession or control of data, ensuring accountability.

questions.q: Which regulatory requirement most directly demands proof of data provenance?
options: WCAG accessibility guidelines
GDPR's requirement to demonstrate lawful basis for processing and data accuracy
HTTP/2 protocol compliance
DNS record management
questions.explanation: GDPR requires organisations to demonstrate that personal data is accurate, lawfully obtained, and properly handled. Data provenance records are essential for proving compliance during audits.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'I'm seeing that the customer ID used here was generated by the `UserCreationService`. Before merging, can you add a comment documenting *where* this ID came from and *when* it was created? It's crucial for debugging future issues with user accounts.' Which of the following best describes what Reviewer is asking for in this context?
options: insufficient - the account balance is too low...
incorrect - the customer ID should be randomly generated.
complete documentation of data provenance, including source and creation timestamp.
unnecessary - all code should automatically track its lineage.
questions.explanation: The reviewer isn't simply asking for a random comment; they're specifically requesting information about the origin of the customer ID - where it was generated (the `UserCreationService`) and when (creation timestamp). This highlights the importance of 'data provenance', which is understanding *how* data originated and its history. The incorrect options either misunderstand the request or offer a simplistic view that ignores the critical need for traceability in software development.

questions.q: A developer is reviewing a PR that uses the get_user_data function. The code comments mention 'provenance' and 'tracking data lineage.' What does this likely refer to? This ensures we can trace where the user data originated .
options: A complete audit of all user data processing steps.
The ability to track the origin and transformations of data throughout its lifecycle.
Strict adherence to GDPR regulations regarding user privacy.
Optimizing database queries for faster user data retrieval.
questions.explanation: 'Data provenance' refers to the ability to trace a piece of data back to its source and understand all the steps it has undergone. It's about tracking the entire journey of the data, not just enforcing regulations or optimizing performance. Options A & D are too broad; option B is the most accurate definition.

questions.q: During a standup meeting, a developer says, "We need to ensure the data from our new analytics pipeline has strong provenance." What's the primary concern driving this statement?
options: A desire for faster reporting speeds.
The need to comply with strict legal regulations regarding data accuracy.
A commitment to maintaining a high level of data quality and trust.
Ensuring the analytics team can easily debug any issues.
questions.explanation: Strong data provenance is crucial when dealing with sensitive or regulated data. It's not just about speed; it's about accountability and verifying that the data used in analytics is reliable and trustworthy. Option A & D are misinterpretations of the core concept.

questions.q: A senior engineer asks you to add a field to your API response that records the original source of a product's price. What is the primary purpose of this addition related to 'data provenance'? This helps with debugging and understanding data transformations .
options: To reduce the size of the API response.
To provide users with more detailed pricing information.
To simplify the API documentation for developers.
To enable automated price comparison across different vendors.
questions.explanation: Adding provenance details allows you to trace back how a product's price was calculated. This is vital for debugging issues, understanding data transformations, and ensuring accuracy. Options B & D are related to API design but don't address the core concept of provenance.

questions.q: You're investigating a discrepancy in sales figures. The data originated from a third-party CRM system. Which of the following best describes how 'data lineage' would be most helpful in your investigation? </strong
options: Providing a detailed report on the CRM system's performance metrics.
Mapping out the entire path of the sales data from the CRM to your internal systems, including all transformations and calculations.
Offering suggestions for improving the accuracy of the CRM's data entry fields.
Analyzing customer demographics to identify potential biases in the sales figures.
questions.explanation: 'Data lineage' focuses on understanding the entire journey of the data - where it came from, how it was modified, and what systems it passed through. This is essential for identifying the root cause of discrepancies. Options A & D are tangential to the core concept.

questions.q: A data governance team mandates that all customer data be tracked with a 'provenance record'. What is the MOST important reason for this requirement? </strong
options: To simplify the process of generating marketing reports.
To ensure compliance with industry regulations and maintain accountability for data quality.
To improve the performance of database queries used to access customer data.
To reduce the risk of human error in data entry.
questions.explanation: Data provenance is fundamentally about accountability and trust. Tracking the origin and transformations of data is crucial for complying with regulations (like GDPR or CCPA), demonstrating responsible data handling practices, and ensuring that decisions are based on reliable information. Options A & D are secondary benefits.

exercises.title: Data Quality & Lineage Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for data quality dimensions (completeness, accuracy, timeliness, consistency, uniqueness), data quality rules, expectations, data SLA, and anomaly detection.

questions.q: The data quality dimension "completeness" measures:
options: Whether all required business logic has been applied to transform raw data correctly.
The proportion of expected data that is actually present - detecting missing records, null values in required fields, or gaps in time-series data that should have continuous coverage.
Whether a dataset covers all the business domains required for a comprehensive analysis.
The degree to which data captures the full history of events without gaps in lineage.
questions.explanation: Completeness example: "email is null for 12% of user records - expected 0% null rate." Or: "pipeline delivered 8,200 rows today; expected 10,000 ± 5%. Missing 18% of expected volume." Completeness checks are the most common first line of data quality monitoring.

questions.q: The data quality dimension "timeliness" refers to:
options: The speed at which data pipelines process and transform data from source to destination.
Whether data is available when consumers need it - data that arrives after the business deadline (report generation, end-of-day processing) has failed its timeliness SLA even if it is accurate.
The time it takes for data quality checks to complete and publish their results.
How quickly a data quality incident is detected and resolved after it occurs.
questions.explanation: Timeliness is distinct from freshness: fresh data arrived recently; timely data arrived before the deadline. Example: "sales reports must reflect all transactions by 08:00 UTC for the morning leadership review." A pipeline completing at 09:00 with accurate data still fails its timeliness SLA.

questions.q: In Great Expectations terminology, an "expectation" is:
options: A business requirement document specifying the expected behaviour of a data pipeline.

A declarative, testable assertion about data - such as "column email must not be null", "column age must be between 0 and 120", or "column user_id must be unique" - validated automatically on each pipeline run.
A service level expectation defining how quickly a data team must respond to quality issues.
A predicted value range generated by a machine learning model for anomaly detection.
questions.explanation: Great Expectations (GX) provides a Python framework for writing data expectations as code. Expectations are run as part of pipelines and produce Validation Results: pass/fail per expectation. A Data Doc summarises results for stakeholders. This approach makes data quality testable and version-controlled.

questions.q: A "data SLA" (Service Level Agreement) in a data context defines:
options: A legal contract between a data vendor and a company specifying data delivery guarantees.
A commitment to data consumers about quality, freshness, and availability - for example: "the orders table will be updated by 07:00 UTC daily, with completeness ≥ 99.5% and zero duplicate order IDs."
An agreement between data engineering and security teams about encryption standards.
The percentage of uptime guaranteed for a data warehouse or data lake platform.
questions.explanation: Data SLAs make implicit quality expectations explicit and measurable. They enable SLO tracking (Service Level Objectives) and incident alerting: "orders SLA breached - data is 2 hours late". Without data SLAs, consumers discover failures only when reports are wrong, long after the pipeline missed its window.

questions.q: Data anomaly detection in the context of data quality lineage means:
options: Using machine learning to detect fraud patterns in transactional data.

Automatically identifying unexpected deviations from historical norms in pipeline outputs - such as a sudden 60% drop in daily row count, an unusual spike in null rates, or a metric value outside its historical distribution.
Detecting anomalies in the data lineage graph caused by schema changes in upstream tables.
Identifying unusual query patterns that may indicate unauthorised data access.
questions.explanation: ML-based anomaly detection (Monte Carlo, Acceldata, Anomalo) learns baseline distributions for metrics like row count, null rate, and column value ranges - then alerts when actual values deviate significantly. This catches quality regressions that static threshold rules miss, particularly for metrics with seasonal patterns.

exercises.title: GDPR Right-to-Erasure via Lineage Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for GDPR right-to-erasure workflows using data lineage: deleting user records, propagating deletions downstream, and compliance documentation language.

questions.q: The GDPR "right to erasure" (also called "right to be forgotten") requires organisations to:
options: Archive all data about a user into a secure cold-storage location within 30 days of their account deletion.
Delete all personal data held about an individual upon their request - across every system, backup, and derived dataset where that data exists - unless a lawful basis for retention applies.
Anonymise user data by replacing names with pseudonyms while retaining the rest of the record.
Provide users with a downloadable export of all their data before deleting their account.
questions.explanation: GDPR Article 17 grants individuals the right to request deletion of their personal data. The obligation is comprehensive - not just the primary database, but all downstream derived tables, aggregations, backups (within reasonable timescales), data warehouse copies, ML training datasets, and third-party processors. Data lineage is essential here: without knowing every system where user X's data exists, you cannot reliably fulfill the erasure request. Failure can result in fines of up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover.

questions.q: When an engineer says "delete all records for user X", in a GDPR lineage context this means:
options: Running a single DELETE statement on the primary users table in the production database.

Identifying every dataset in the lineage graph that contains data derived from or linked to user X's records, then deleting or suppressing that data across all systems - and documenting the process for compliance.
Deactivating user X's account so they can no longer log in to the application.
Anonymising user X's data by replacing their personal identifiers with a random UUID.
questions.explanation: "Delete all records for user X" in a GDPR context is a multi-system operation. Using lineage, you traverse forward from the source (e.g., raw.users) to find every downstream table that joins on user_id. This may include: staging tables, mart tables, ML feature stores, event logs, BI dashboards, data exports, and third-party integrations. Each must be addressed. Many organisations maintain an "erasure service" that uses lineage metadata to orchestrate this automatically.

questions.q: "Propagate deletion downstream" in a data lineage workflow means:
options: Notifying downstream data consumers via email that a user's data has been deleted from the source system.

Using the lineage graph to trigger deletion or suppression of a user's personal data in every dependent dataset after removing it from the source - ensuring no derived copy retains identifiable information.
Rerunning all downstream pipelines after a deletion so they recalculate their aggregations without the deleted user.
Propagating a database transaction rollback across distributed systems to undo accidental deletions.
questions.explanation: Deletion propagation is the downstream equivalent of data propagation. If user X's row is deleted from raw.users, the lineage graph shows that stg.users, dim.customers, fct.orders (joined on customer_id), and the churn prediction feature table all contain derived data. Each must be updated - either by re-running the pipeline (if idempotent), running targeted DELETE/UPDATE statements, or applying a suppression flag. The lineage graph is the map that makes this tractable at scale.

questions.q: Compliance documentation language for a GDPR erasure request typically includes:
options: A Git commit message summarising the SQL statements run to delete the user's data.

A formal record stating: the erasure request received date, the user identifier, every system where data was found and deleted (with timestamps), confirmation that no lawful retention basis applied, and the date the request was fulfilled - stored in an auditable compliance log.
A screenshot of the database query results showing zero rows returned after deletion.
An internal Slack thread confirming that the engineering team has handled the deletion request.
questions.explanation: GDPR erasure compliance requires auditable documentation. A complete record should include: (1) date and channel of the erasure request, (2) identity verification steps taken, (3) list of systems searched (derived from lineage), (4) confirmation of deletion in each system with timestamps, (5) any data retained under lawful basis with justification, (6) date the requester was notified of completion. This documentation must be retained (paradoxically) to demonstrate GDPR compliance, but must not itself contain the deleted personal data.

questions.q: Which approach best uses data lineage to fulfill a GDPR erasure request at scale?
options: Asking each team to manually check their databases for the user's data and confirm deletion.

Using the data catalog's lineage graph to automatically identify all datasets containing the user's data by tracing downstream from the PII source tables, then triggering an automated erasure workflow that deletes or suppresses the data in each system and logs each action to a compliance audit trail.
Deleting the user from the primary application database and relying on downstream pipelines to naturally exclude them in the next run.
Anonymising the user's record in the source system and waiting for downstream tables to refresh with anonymised data.
questions.explanation: At scale - when a data platform has hundreds of datasets - manual erasure is impractical and error-prone. Lineage-driven erasure automation is the mature approach: (1) lineage graph identifies all affected datasets, (2) each dataset's owner is notified or an automated job is triggered, (3) deletions are logged centrally, (4) a completion audit report is generated. Companies like Databricks, Snowflake, and various DaaS vendors are building native erasure capabilities that leverage lineage metadata for exactly this workflow.

exercises.title: Data Governance Communication Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for data governance frameworks, governance committees, RACI for data, federated governance models, data mesh governance, data policies, and standards.

questions.q: A data governance framework defines:
options: The technical architecture for storing and processing data across an organisation.
The policies, processes, roles, and standards that govern how data is created, managed, used, and protected - ensuring data is trustworthy, accessible, and compliant with regulations.
A software framework for automating data pipeline orchestration and quality checks.
The organisational structure of the data engineering team and their reporting lines.
questions.explanation: Data governance frameworks (DAMA-DMBOK, IBM Data Governance Council model) define: who owns data, who can access it, how quality is measured, how policies are enforced. Without a framework, governance is ad-hoc and inconsistent - different teams apply different standards to the same data.

questions.q: A data governance committee typically does:
options: Reviews and approves technical architecture decisions for data infrastructure investments.

Brings together data owners, stewards, legal, compliance, and business representatives to set data policies, resolve cross-domain conflicts, approve access requests, and oversee governance programme health.
Conducts regular data quality audits and reports findings to the engineering team.
Manages the budget allocation for data tools and cloud infrastructure spending.
questions.explanation: Data governance committees (also called Data Councils or Data Governance Boards) are the decision-making body for data policies. They handle escalations: "Which team owns the definition of 'customer'?", "Should we allow external access to this dataset?", "What is our retention policy for clickstream data?"

questions.q: A RACI matrix for data governance assigns:
options: The technical components (R=Repository, A=API, C=Catalog, I=Integration) of a data platform.

Responsibility, Accountability, Consultation, and Information roles for data activities - clarifying who makes decisions, who does the work, who is consulted, and who is informed for each data process.
Risk levels (R=Red, A=Amber, C=Clear, I=Immaterial) to individual datasets based on their sensitivity.
Resource Allocation, Cost, and Impact scores for data governance programme initiatives.
questions.explanation: RACI for data example: for "approving access to PII dataset" - R: data steward (does the review), A: data owner (accountable for the decision), C: legal (consulted on compliance), I: IT security (informed of the decision). RACI prevents "everyone assumes someone else is handling it."

questions.q: A "federated governance model" in a data mesh context means:
options: Governance managed entirely by a central data platform team with full authority over all domains.

Governance distributed across domain teams who own and govern their own data products, within a set of global standards and a computational governance layer enforced by the platform - autonomy with guardrails.
A governance model where data is federated across multiple cloud providers to avoid vendor lock-in.
A federated database architecture where governance rules are applied at query time across distributed sources.
questions.explanation: Federated governance balances central control with domain autonomy: the central platform team sets global policies (PII classification standards, retention policies, naming conventions), but each domain team applies and enforces them for their own data products. This avoids both the bottleneck of centralised governance and the chaos of no governance.

questions.q: A "data standard" in governance communication refers to:
options: A benchmark score indicating the minimum acceptable level of data quality for a dataset.

A documented, organisation-wide rule about how data should be structured, named, formatted, or managed - for example: "all timestamps must use UTC", "customer IDs must follow the format CUST-XXXXXXXX", "every dataset must have a named owner in the catalog."
An industry certification standard (ISO, SOC 2) applied to data management practices.
A standardised report template used for communicating data metrics to executives.
questions.explanation: Data standards prevent the chaos of inconsistency: if one team stores dates as DD/MM/YYYY and another as YYYY-MM-DD, joins fail silently. Standards must be documented, enforced (via linting, catalog validation), and socialised. Common standards: naming conventions, data type standards, timezone standards, classification taxonomies.

exercises.title: Lineage-Driven Debugging Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practice lineage-driven debugging vocabulary: tracing NULLs upstream, metric drops, broken field investigation, and root cause analysis using data lineage.

questions.q: An engineer says 'we used lineage to find where the ___ came from.' What data quality issue are they debugging?
options: index
NULL
partition
schema
questions.explanation: NULL values propagating through a pipeline are a classic data quality issue. Lineage lets engineers trace a NULL back through transformations to the source table or pipeline step where it was introduced.

questions.q: A metric dropped 20% overnight. The correct lineage-driven debugging step is to:
options: Restart all pipeline jobs immediately
Check the lineage graph to identify which upstream source table or transformation changed
Increase the compute resources for the pipeline
Send an alert to all data consumers
questions.explanation: Lineage-driven debugging starts with the lineage graph: trace the affected metric back through its dependencies to find which upstream source or transformation was updated around the time the drop occurred.

questions.q: What does 'trace the broken field upstream' mean?
options: Push the broken field to downstream consumers
Follow the lineage graph backwards from the broken field to find where it was last correct
Delete the field and recreate it
Update the field's data type in the schema
questions.explanation: Tracing upstream means following the lineage graph in reverse - from the broken output field back through each transformation step - to identify the earliest point where the data was incorrect.

questions.q: 'Root cause analysis using lineage' means:
options: Analysing the root file system of the data warehouse
Using the lineage graph to systematically identify the original source of a data problem
Calculating the average latency of root-level pipeline jobs
Auditing root-level database permissions
questions.explanation: In data debugging, root cause analysis using lineage means following the dependency graph backwards to find the ultimate origin of a data quality issue - not just the symptom but the actual cause.

questions.q: A colleague says: 'The lineage shows the source table was ___ at 2am - that explains the metric drop.' What word fits?
options: archived
updated
encrypted
replicated
questions.explanation: When a source table is updated (new data loaded, rows changed, or schema modified), it can cause unexpected changes in downstream metrics. Lineage timestamps help correlate source updates with downstream anomalies.

questions.q: PR Title: Fix: Incorrect Order Calculation During a code review, Sarah comments on David's PR: "David, I'm seeing an issue with the order calculation. The lineage shows that the `order_total` value is being derived from a calculated field in the `discount_engine` service. However, the discount engine itself relies on a legacy table, `legacy_customer_data`, which has known inconsistencies. It looks like we need to trace the broken field upstream to understand where these discrepancies are originating."
options: Identify the specific SQL query that calculates the `order_total` and optimize its performance.
Implement a new data validation rule at the point of origin in legacy_customer_data to ensure accurate data is being loaded.
Investigate whether the discount engine service is correctly consuming data from legacy_customer_data , focusing on potential schema mismatches or transformation errors.
Request a full audit of all changes made to the `discount_engine` service over the past six months.
questions.explanation: This question assesses understanding of 'trace the broken field upstream.' The core concept is that when debugging lineage-driven issues, you must follow the data flow backwards from the point where a problem manifests. Option 2 correctly identifies this process - focusing on validating the source data and transformation logic. Options 1 and 4 are irrelevant to the immediate issue of incorrect calculations; option 3 is too broad and doesn't specifically address tracing the lineage.

questions.q: During a Slack conversation about a recent spike in failed payments, Ben says: 'Okay, let's use lineage to see where this payment data is originating. I want to trace the broken field upstream and identify any issues with the initial input.' What is Ben primarily attempting to achieve by requesting this action?
options: To immediately fix the faulty payment processing code within the discount engine service.
To investigate potential errors in the legacy customer data table that are propagating through the system's calculations.
To determine if the issue is isolated to a single user's transaction or widespread across all payments.
To identify whether the order calculation logic itself is flawed, regardless of its data sources.
questions.explanation: Ben is utilizing lineage-driven debugging to pinpoint the root of the problem by examining the data's journey. He wants to trace the broken field upstream, meaning he's focused on identifying the source table-likely the legacy customer data-where the initial inconsistencies are introduced and then propagated through subsequent calculations. This approach contrasts with simply fixing the discount engine code; it addresses the underlying cause of the issue rather than treating a symptom.

questions.q: During a standup update, John reports: "We've been seeing intermittent errors in the reporting dashboard. The lineage analysis reveals that the problematic data originates from a transformation within the `reporting_service`. Specifically, the value for 'customer_segment' is being derived from a lookup table called 'marketing_segments'. To investigate further, I need to trace the broken field upstream to pinpoint the source of this faulty transformation."
options: Identify potential bugs in the reporting service logic.
Investigate whether the marketing_segments table has outdated definitions.
Determine if there are any data quality issues affecting the original source of the customer segment data.
Immediately roll back the changes made to the reporting service.
questions.explanation: The question focuses on tracing the lineage . While bugs in the `reporting_service` could be a factor, the lineage analysis specifically points to an issue with the `marketing_segments` table. Therefore, the correct action is to investigate whether the marketing segments have outdated definitions, as this is where the problem originates based on the provided information. Options A and B are possible contributing factors, but tracing upstream is the most direct method to address the root cause identified by the lineage.

exercises.title: Impact Analysis Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for impact analysis in data lineage: downstream dependencies, breaking change propagation, and communicating schema changes to pipeline stakeholders.

questions.q: When a data engineer says "what downstream datasets depend on this table?", they are performing:
options: A data quality audit to check freshness and completeness of the table.
An impact analysis - using the lineage graph to identify every consumer that will be affected if this table changes or becomes unavailable.
A schema migration to rename columns before deprecating the original table.
A cost analysis to determine which downstream jobs consume the most compute.
questions.explanation: "What downstream datasets depend on this?" is the defining impact analysis question in data lineage work. The answer comes from traversing the lineage graph forward from the node in question. Modern data catalogs (DataHub, Atlan, OpenMetadata) surface this as a "downstream lineage" panel. Engineers use this before schema changes, deprecations, or SLA negotiations.

questions.q: A "breaking change" in the context of a data pipeline means:
options: A change to a pipeline's schedule that shifts its run time to a different hour.
A modification to a source table - such as renaming or removing a column - that causes one or more downstream models or jobs to fail or produce incorrect results.
A network outage that temporarily interrupts data flow between systems.
A change in business logic approved by stakeholders that intentionally alters output metrics.
questions.explanation: Breaking changes in data pipelines are analogous to breaking API changes in software. Removing a column, changing its data type, or renaming it can silently break dbt models, SQL queries, and dashboards that reference it. Impact analysis via lineage helps engineers know in advance which consumers will break, so they can coordinate changes or maintain backward compatibility.

questions.q: The phrase "this schema change will affect N pipelines" is typically communicated by:
options: The database administrator who applies the migration directly in production.
An automated lineage tool or data catalog that counts all downstream jobs referencing the changed table or column, giving stakeholders a concrete scope before any change is made.
The BI analyst who manually checks each dashboard for broken data sources.
The on-call engineer who discovers breakages after the deployment.
questions.explanation: Modern lineage tools (DataHub's impact analysis, Atlan's change impact, dbt's --select downstream notation) can enumerate exactly how many pipelines, models, and dashboards reference a given field. Communicating "this rename will affect 14 downstream models and 3 dashboards" allows teams to plan coordinated changes - or choose additive approaches (new column + deprecation notice) instead.

questions.q: Change propagation in data lineage refers to:
options: Broadcasting a data schema update announcement to all team members via email.
The process by which a change at one node in the data pipeline - whether a schema change, a data quality issue, or a logic update - flows forward through all dependent downstream datasets.
Synchronising data between a primary database and its read replicas.
The mechanism by which version control commits are deployed to production pipelines.
questions.explanation: Change propagation describes how effects ripple through a lineage graph. If raw.orders loses a column, the effect propagates: staging.orders breaks → mart.revenue breaks → the finance dashboard shows nulls. Understanding propagation depth - how many hops downstream - helps teams triage incidents and plan migrations. Tools like dbt's dag visualisation make propagation paths explicit.

questions.q: Which phrase best communicates a safe approach to a breaking schema change?
options: "I will rename the column tonight and send a message to the channel afterwards."
"I will add the new column alongside the old one, mark the old column as deprecated in the catalog, notify downstream owners, and remove it only after all consumers have migrated."
"I will update the column and then run all downstream jobs to see which ones fail."
"I will roll back the change immediately if anyone reports an issue in the next 48 hours."
questions.explanation: The recommended pattern for breaking schema changes is: (1) add the new column or table additively, (2) mark the old field as deprecated in the data catalog, (3) notify downstream owners identified through impact analysis, (4) agree on a migration window, (5) remove only after all consumers have updated. This avoids silent failures and respects SLAs of dependent teams.

exercises.title: Data Lineage Review Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for presenting data lineage findings: lineage graph interpretation, column-level lineage, trust scores, and communicating lineage insights to stakeholders.

questions.q: When a data engineer says "the lineage graph shows", they are about to:
options: Display a bar chart of pipeline execution times for performance review.

Present a visual or structured representation of how data flows between datasets - showing source tables, transformation steps, and downstream consumers - to explain a data dependency, an incident root cause, or an impact scope.
Show a network diagram of the database servers and their replication topology.
Present a schema diagram of foreign key relationships between database tables.
questions.explanation: "The lineage graph shows..." is a standard opening phrase when presenting lineage findings to colleagues or stakeholders. It signals that what follows is derived from the actual dependency graph - not from memory or assumption. Examples: "The lineage graph shows that this dashboard's revenue metric traces back through three transformation layers to raw.stripe_events", or "The lineage graph shows 12 downstream models will be affected by this schema change". The phrase establishes evidence-based communication.

questions.q: "Column-level lineage confirms" is used when:
options: A database administrator verifies that all column constraints are correctly defined in the schema.

A data engineer or analyst uses column-level lineage data to prove - not just assert - that a specific output column is derived from specific source columns through specific transformations, providing precise traceability for a metric or data quality finding.
A BI developer confirms that column names in a dashboard match the underlying warehouse schema.
A data steward verifies that all sensitive columns have been correctly classified in the catalog.
questions.explanation: "Column-level lineage confirms that revenue_usd in the executive dashboard is computed from amount_cents in raw.stripe_charges, divided by 100, filtered where status = 'succeeded', and summed by month" - this is the kind of statement column-level lineage enables. It elevates a data review from table-level ("this comes from Stripe") to field-level precision. Tools that provide column-level lineage: dbt column lineage, Atlan, DataHub, OpenLineage with field-level events.

questions.q: A "trust score" for a dataset in a lineage review context typically measures:
options: The number of engineers who have reviewed and approved the dataset's code.

A composite indicator - combining data quality check pass rates, freshness, documentation completeness, and lineage coverage - that helps consumers quickly assess whether a dataset is reliable enough to use for a specific purpose.
The security clearance level required to access the dataset.
The percentage of queries against the dataset that returned results within the SLA response time.
questions.explanation: Trust score (used in Atlan, and conceptually in many governance tools) aggregates signals: recent quality checks passed (%), documentation completeness (%), lineage coverage (are sources documented?), certification status, and usage activity. When presenting lineage findings, referencing a trust score gives stakeholders a shorthand: "The source table has a trust score of 87% - quality checks are passing but documentation is incomplete." It contextualises confidence in the lineage path being reviewed.

questions.q: Which phrase correctly presents a lineage finding to a non-technical stakeholder?
options: "The DAG shows node raw__orders has an edge to stg__orders which joins to fct__revenue via a surrogate key."

"The lineage graph shows that the monthly revenue figure in your dashboard originates from the orders system, passes through two cleaning steps, and is then aggregated - meaning any data quality issue in the orders system will affect the revenue numbers within 24 hours."
"There's a dependency chain: raw.orders → stg.orders → mart.revenue → BI layer."
"Column-level lineage confirms that amount_cents flows through a /100 transformation into revenue_usd with a COMPLETED status filter."
questions.explanation: When presenting lineage findings to non-technical stakeholders, translate graph concepts into business language: "originates from the orders system" instead of "upstream node raw.orders", "passes through two cleaning steps" instead of "intermediate transformation layers", "affect the revenue numbers within 24 hours" instead of "propagate downstream within one pipeline execution cycle". The lineage insight is the same - but the framing matches the audience. Technical precision (options A, C, D) is appropriate for engineer-to-engineer communication.

questions.q: When documenting lineage review findings in a data incident report, which structure is most appropriate?
options: A list of SQL queries run during the investigation, with their execution times.

A structured narrative that includes: the affected dataset, the lineage path traced from source to impact, the root cause node identified in the graph, the downstream datasets confirmed as affected, the column-level lineage that pinpointed the transformation where the issue was introduced, and recommended remediation steps.
A screenshot of the lineage graph with a comment that says "issue found here" with an arrow.
A Slack message summarising what went wrong, sent to the data team channel.
questions.explanation: A lineage-informed data incident report follows a structured pattern: (1) Affected output - what the business saw (wrong revenue, missing rows), (2) Lineage path - the full graph from source to output, (3) Root cause node - where the issue was introduced (upstream schema change, pipeline failure, bad transformation), (4) Affected scope - downstream datasets confirmed impacted via lineage traversal, (5) Column-level evidence - which specific field carried the error, (6) Remediation - fix at the root cause, then verify downstream datasets correct themselves. This structure enables future root cause analysis and builds organisational lineage knowledge.

exercises.title: Metadata Management Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for technical vs. business metadata, operational metadata, schema metadata, metadata-driven architecture, and data classification labels (PII, confidential, public).

questions.q: Technical metadata in a data catalog includes:
options: Business definitions, glossary terms, and ownership information about datasets.
Structural information about data assets: table schemas, column data types, row counts, file sizes, partition structures, and storage locations - the "what is it technically?" layer.
Notes and comments added by analysts describing how a dataset should be interpreted.
Lineage graphs showing how datasets are transformed through data pipelines.
questions.explanation: Technical metadata is harvested automatically by catalog crawlers: column names, data types, nullability, partitioning, row counts, table size, last modified timestamp. Business metadata (descriptions, glossary links, ownership) must be added by humans. Both are needed for a complete picture.

questions.q: Operational metadata about a dataset refers to:
options: Metadata describing how the data should be used in operational business processes.
Runtime information about data pipeline executions: last run timestamp, run duration, rows processed, error rates, SLA compliance - the health and recency signals for a data asset.
Information about the operational costs associated with storing and querying a dataset.
The access logs recording which users and applications have read a dataset.
questions.explanation: Operational metadata tells you: "Is this data fresh? When was the pipeline last run? Did the last run succeed? How many rows were loaded?" Modern catalogs surface operational metadata alongside technical and business metadata, so analysts can judge data freshness before using it.

questions.q: A "metadata-driven architecture" means:
options: An architecture where all data is stored as metadata rather than in structured tables.

A design approach where system behaviour (pipeline logic, schema migrations, access controls, transformations) is controlled by metadata configuration rather than hardcoded logic - making systems more flexible and self-documenting.
An architecture optimised for storing and querying large volumes of metadata efficiently.
A microservices architecture where each service is documented using OpenAPI metadata.
questions.explanation: Example: a metadata-driven ingestion framework reads configuration from a metadata store ("ingest table X from source Y, using schema Z, with incremental key updated_at") and generates the pipeline automatically. Adding a new table means updating metadata, not writing new code - dramatically reducing engineering effort.

questions.q: PII (Personally Identifiable Information) as a data classification label means:
options: Data that is considered proprietary and internally confidential to the organisation.

Data that can identify a specific individual - such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, IP addresses, or device IDs - requiring special access controls, retention limits, and GDPR/CCPA compliance handling.
Data that is personally curated and maintained by individual data stewards.
Data that is in a personally-owned dataset rather than an organisationally-managed one.
questions.explanation: PII classification in catalogs drives automated governance: PII-tagged columns trigger masking in non-production environments, restrict access to authorised roles, are included in right-to-erasure workflows, and must be documented in data processing agreements. Without PII tagging, compliance is manual and error-prone.

questions.q: Data freshness metadata in a catalog context refers to:
options: A quality score indicating whether the data in a table is accurate and free of errors.
Information about when a dataset was last updated and whether it meets its expected update frequency - helping consumers know if data is current enough for their use case before querying it.
A certificate indicating that a dataset has been recently reviewed and approved by its steward.
Metadata about the age of data records, indicating whether records are current or historical.
questions.explanation: Freshness metadata example: "orders_daily was last refreshed 3 hours ago; expected refresh is daily at 06:00 UTC; last 7 days: 6/7 on-time." A consumer planning a report can see immediately whether the data is stale. Catalogs that surface freshness prevent analysts from presenting yesterday's data as today's.

exercises.title: Operational Data Lineage Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practice operational data lineage vocabulary: tracing data from source to report, lineage-based impact analysis, pipeline break investigation, and field semantics vocabulary.

questions.q: An engineer says 'the pipeline broke here - lineage shows the ___ source.' What word fits?
options: downstream
upstream
parallel
cached
questions.explanation: In lineage, 'upstream' refers to earlier stages in the data flow - the sources that feed a broken stage. Lineage tools let engineers quickly identify which upstream source caused a failure.

questions.q: What is 'lineage-based impact analysis'?
options: Measuring query performance across the pipeline
Using lineage graphs to identify which downstream reports or datasets will be affected by a change to an upstream source
Tracking how long data takes to move through the pipeline
Auditing who accessed a dataset
questions.explanation: Lineage-based impact analysis uses the lineage graph to trace all downstream dependencies. Before changing a table or field, engineers can see which reports, models, or consumers would be affected.

questions.q: The phrase 'tracing data from source to report' describes which lineage concept?
options: Data masking
End-to-end lineage
Schema evolution
Data partitioning
questions.explanation: End-to-end lineage means being able to follow data from its original source (e.g., a transactional database) all the way through transformations to its final destination (e.g., a business report).

questions.q: A colleague says 'the transformation changed the ___ of this field.' What word means the intended meaning of the data?
options: index
semantics
partition
schema
questions.explanation: 'Semantics' refers to the meaning of data. Transformations can change semantics without changing the field name - e.g., a 'revenue' field might change from gross to net revenue. Lineage helps detect these semantic shifts.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses operational lineage vocabulary?
options: We used lineage to scale the pipeline horizontally.
We ran lineage to find which upstream table introduced the NULL values in the report.
Lineage compressed the dataset by 40%.
We disabled lineage to speed up the ETL job.
questions.explanation: Operational lineage is used to investigate data issues - finding where NULLs, incorrect values, or unexpected changes were introduced by tracing data flow through the pipeline graph.

questions.q: During a code review of the new payment processing service, Sarah commented: 'I'm seeing inconsistent values in the reports. The lineage shows that this data originated from the `TransactionService` API. Can we investigate where the transformation is introducing these discrepancies?' Which word best describes what Sarah is asking for when she references the 'lineage' of the data?
options: schema
metadata
transformation
validation
questions.explanation: Sarah is seeking to understand the specific changes that were made to the data as it flowed through the system. Metadata refers to the data about the data - in this case, information describing how the `TransactionService` API's output was processed and altered. Options A, B, and C are all related to different aspects of data management but don't capture Sarah's focus on tracing the *process* of change itself. Incorrectly thinking of 'schema' as the answer suggests a structural definition, while the problem is about how the data has been modified.

questions.q: PR Description: "Fix: Updated the customer address validation logic. This PR now uses the new `AddressService` to ensure all addresses are compliant with GDPR regulations. Lineage impacts are minimal - only the source data for customer profiles is affected."
options: schema
transformation
metadata
source
questions.explanation: The PR description highlights that the primary impact of this change relates to where the data originates. Metadata refers to the information *about* the data-in this case, it's describing the source and its compliance rules. Options A, B, and C are all related to how the data is manipulated or defined; understanding the initial source is critical for impact analysis and debugging.

questions.q: John : 'The data quality team flagged an issue with the new sales dashboard. The lineage report indicates a change occurred in the `CustomerSegmentationService`'s transformation logic. We need to understand exactly what that change did to the underlying customer data.' Which of the following terms best describes John 's request for clarification regarding the transformation's effect?
options: Data validation
Schema evolution
Metadata propagation
Operational impact
questions.explanation: John is asking about the consequences of a change in the transformation logic. 'Operational impact' correctly identifies this - it refers to how a change affects the *flow* and processing of data throughout the system's operational lineage. The other options-data validation, schema evolution, and metadata propagation-describe different aspects of data management but don't capture the core concern about the transformation's effect on live data in a production environment.

questions.q: {code snippet: PR Description} During a discussion about a recent code change to the order processing system, David states, 'The lineage report shows that the new `OrderValidationService` is pulling data directly from the legacy `OrdersDB` table. This seems like a significant shift - we should investigate potential downstream impacts.' Which term best describes David's concern regarding this lineage information?
options: Anomaly
Correlation
Impact
Variance
questions.explanation: David is concerned about the 'impact' of a change in data lineage. Specifically, he recognizes that pulling data directly from an older database table - which may have different schemas or data quality issues - could lead to unexpected errors or inconsistencies downstream. 'Anomaly' and 'Variance' refer to deviations from expected values; 'Correlation' describes a statistical relationship between variables, neither of which is relevant to David's concern about the change itself. Understanding lineage impacts is key to assessing potential risks.

questions.q: // Slack Message Alex (DevOps): "Hey team, we've got a spike in errors with the reporting dashboard. The lineage graph shows a recent change to the `ProductCatalogService` transformation." Which of the following best describes Alex's concern regarding this lineage information?
options: Anomaly - it's an unexpected deviation from normal behavior.
Root Cause - identifying the fundamental reason for the problem.
Impact Assessment - evaluating the extent to which the change affects downstream systems.
Data Drift - a gradual change in the statistical properties of a dataset over time.
questions.explanation: Alex is using 'Root Cause' to describe his concern. The lineage graph highlights a recent transformation, and he's seeking to understand *why* that transformation might be causing errors in the reporting dashboard. 'Anomaly' refers to unexpected behavior generally; 'Impact Assessment' focuses on scope, and 'Data Drift' describes a different phenomenon related to data changes over time. Identifying the root cause of the issue is his immediate priority.

exercises.title: Data Stewardship Communication Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for data stewardship workflows: data ownership, access requests, data classification, and stewardship communication in governance contexts.

questions.q: When someone says "who is the data owner?", they are asking:
options: Which cloud account holds billing responsibility for the storage costs of the dataset.
Which person or team has formal accountability for the dataset's business accuracy, quality, and appropriate use - the individual who approves access and answers governance questions.
Which data engineer wrote the original pipeline that populates the dataset.
Which database administrator has superuser privileges on the schema containing the table.
questions.explanation: "Data owner" is a governance role, not a technical one. The data owner is accountable for the dataset's fitness for purpose: they define who may access it, what it should contain, and they sign off on its certified status. In RACI terms, they are Accountable (A). They are typically a domain lead, product manager, or senior analyst - not the engineer who built the pipeline. Knowing who the data owner is before requesting access or raising quality issues is standard governance practice.

questions.q: The phrase "I'm requesting access to [dataset]" initiates:
options: A database query that retrieves sample rows from the dataset for preview.

A formal access request workflow in which the requester justifies their business need, and the data owner or steward reviews and approves or denies access based on data classification and governance policy.
An automated pipeline run that exports the dataset to the requester's personal storage.
A schema documentation pull request that adds the requester as a contributor.
questions.explanation: "Requesting access" in a governed data environment is a structured process - not just a Slack message. Modern data catalogs (Atlan, DataHub, Collibra) have built-in access request workflows: the requester states purpose and duration, the request is routed to the data owner, and access is granted with an expiry. This audit trail is essential for compliance with GDPR, HIPAA, and internal data policies. The phrase "I'm requesting access to" triggers this formal workflow.

questions.q: A data steward's role in a stewardship workflow is best described as:
options: Managing the physical infrastructure - servers, storage, and network - that hosts the data.
Operationally ensuring a dataset's quality, documentation, and metadata are maintained day-to-day - acting as the hands-on manager of data health within the boundaries set by the data owner.
Writing and deploying the ETL pipelines that load data into the warehouse.
Setting the company's overall data strategy and data governance framework at the executive level.
questions.explanation: The data steward is the day-to-day custodian of data quality and governance for a domain or dataset. While the data owner sets accountability and policy, the steward implements it: updating metadata, resolving quality issues, reviewing access requests, maintaining business glossary definitions, and flagging anomalies. In RACI terms, they are often Responsible (R). In large organisations, one owner may have several stewards managing different datasets within their domain.

questions.q: "Data classification" in a stewardship context refers to:
options: Sorting datasets alphabetically or by creation date in the data catalog interface.
Assigning a sensitivity label - such as Public, Internal, Confidential, or Restricted - to a dataset that governs who may access it, how it must be handled, and what protections apply.
Categorising datasets by their technical format, such as CSV, Parquet, or JSON.
Classifying datasets by their business domain (Finance, HR, Marketing) for catalog organisation.
questions.explanation: Data classification is the process of labelling data by sensitivity level. Common classification tiers: Public (freely shareable), Internal (for employees), Confidential (restricted business data), Restricted/PII (personal data requiring GDPR/CCPA controls). Classification determines: who can access, where data may be stored, whether encryption is mandatory, how long it may be retained, and how it must be disposed of. Data stewards apply and maintain these labels in the catalog.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses stewardship vocabulary to communicate a governance concern?
options: "The table is broken and someone needs to fix it urgently before the dashboard loads."

"I've flagged this dataset as containing unclassified PII - the data steward for the customer domain should review and apply the appropriate data classification before we proceed with the analytics use case."
"Can you give me access to the table? I need to run some queries for a report."
"The pipeline failed last night and the data is stale - the on-call engineer should restart it."
questions.explanation: Effective stewardship communication is precise and uses governance vocabulary: "unclassified PII" (the specific problem), "data steward" (the correct role to involve), "customer domain" (the governance scope), "data classification" (the action needed), "analytics use case" (the business context). Compare with the vague alternatives that lack governance framing. In regulated environments, using correct terminology matters for audit trails and accountability.
